THE MINISTER OF CHEMICAL S AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Tabic 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Government fixed the farm gate price of urea and gives 
maximum indicative price for DAP, MOP and complex fertilizers. No 
revision of these prices is envisaged at this juncture. 
(c) Producers of indigenous urea and DAP/complex fertilizers get 
subsidy/concessions to bridge the gap between the selling price at which they 
are required to sell and their cost of production depending on the calculation 
made under Retention Price-cum-Subsidy Scheme in case of urea and the 
Concession Scheme in operation for DAP/ complex fertilizers. A 12% post-
tax return on net worth is built into the RPS. Similarly in the case of 
indigenous DAP, 12% post-tax return on net worth is envisaged while 
determining the cost of production under the Concession Scheme. For 
complex grade fertilizers and SSP, the rate of concession is determined taking 
into account their nutrient content and the concession on per unit of nutrients 
in indigenous DAP and MOP.

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a proposal to re-engineer the education system to

could suit our multi-cultural society and be able to impart the virtues of 
tolerance, etc.  among the citizens? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT, 
MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY AND MINISTER OF 
OCEAN DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
 
27 

RAJYA SABHA       [15 December, 2000] 
Statement 
Educational development is a continuous process. Constant efforts are 
made, from time to time, in consultation with State Governments and other 
stakeholders, and several measures taken to bring about improvements in the 
system to meet the emerging challenges. Several National Resource 
Organisations like the National Institute of Educational Planning and 
Administration (NIPA), National Council of Educational Research and 
Training (NCERT), Indira Gandhi National Open University (IGNOU), 
University Grants Commission (UGC), National Council for Teacher 
Education (NCTC), All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) etc. 
lend their expertise and advice on educational development. 
A number of initiatives have been taken to strengthen school education 
which is the base of the educational pyramid, with impetus being laid on 
Science Education, Environmental Education, Population Education, Culture 
and Values in Education, Computer Literacy and Studies in Schools (CLASS) 
including setting up of smart schools. Education Technology, Education of 
Children with Disabilities and Vocationalisation of Education at the Senior 
Secondary Stage. Besides, the NCERT has been playing a significant role in 
providing resource support in areas of educational research and training at 
school level. A notable development is the National Curriculum Framework 
of School Education recently brought out by NCERT which, inter-alia lays 
stress on the need to modernize school education system to meet the 
challenges of information/ communication technologies and globalisation and 
also on inculcation of value education including inherent values of all 
religions and fundamental duties enshrined in the Constitution. The open 
learning system has played a significant role in the spread of school 
education. It has since been strengthened with the use of modern 
communication technologies. To enlarge the outreach of distance education 
programmes, a separate Television channel '"Gyan Darshan" has been 
operationalised. 'Project Vidya' in association with INTEL has been launched 
for training of teachers and development of curriculum based  software.   
Establishment   of  NCTE   as  a  statutory  body   is 
28 

[15 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
landmark for maintenance of norms and standards in the field of teachers 
education. 
HighLr Education plays a key role in the education system. The National 
Policy on Education (NPE) calls for improvement in the quality of higher 
education, as it  provides people an opportunity to reflect on the critical 
social, economic, cultural and spiritual issues facing them. In the higher 
education sector, establishment of Academic Staff Colleges for training of 
the faculty; Special Assistance Programme for the development of selected 
university departments as Centres of Excellence, strengthening of 
infrastructure in science and technology in collaboration with Indian 
National Science Academy (INSA), autonomous colleges, Information and 
Library Network Programme (INFIBNET) are some of the important 
initiatives for improvement of standards. Establishment of National 
Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) to grade institutions of 
higher education and their programmes is also an important step in this 
direction. UGC has made if mandatory for all universities and colleges to get 
accredited in a time bound manner. A few selected universities are proposed 
to be designated as Universities of Excellence. IGNOU is providing Internet 
education through its computer science programmes, including an Advanced 
Diploma in Information Technology (IT), Bachelor in IT etc. It has network 
of 26 regional centers and over 500 study centers spread all over the country. 
There has been a phenomenal expansion of technical education facilities in 
the country since it is one of the significant components of human resource 
development. Recent initiatives taken to strengthen the technical education 
system include strengthening and consolidation of infrastructural facilities in 
Indian Institutes of Technology (UTs), Indian Institutes of Management 
(IIMs), Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Regional Engineering College 
(RECs) etc; establishment of more UTs, IIMs and engineering colleges; 
establishment of Indian Institute of Information Technology (HIT) at 
Allahabad and Indian Institute of Information Technology & Management   
(IIITM)   at   Gwalior;   increase   of  students   intake   in 
29 

RAJYA SABHA       [15 December, 2000] 
engineering and technical institutions; increasing output of information 
technology manpower; mobilization of private initiatives; development of 
technologies in emerging areas and their transfer to user agencies through 
technology development missions; transfer of techno-economic advances in 
technical education and appropriate technologies to rural people through 
expansion of Community Polytechnics; modernization of institutions and 
development of R&D base through measures like Modernisation and 
Removal of Obsolescence, Research and Development and Thrust Area 
Schemes; World Bank assisted Technician Education Project and Canada 
India Institute Industry Linkage Project; modernization of libraries and switch 
over to electronic libraries with interconnecti-vity; launching of a National 
Education System for Testing (NEST); strengthening of the National Board of 
Accreditation. RECs are being strengthend as per the Mashelkar Committee 
recommendations to be world class institutions (Centres of Excellence). An 
All India Board of IT Education has been constituted under AICTE. 
The NPE recognizes that in our culturally plural society, education 
should foster universal and enternal values, oriented towards the unity and 
integration of our people. Accordingly, measures are being taken to impart 
value education at all stages of education. NCERT has established a National 
Resource Centre for Education in Human Values (EHV) for school education 
sector. The Council has already brought out an exclusive journal on EHV and 
is planning to have a separate website for EHV alone. NCERT will be 
developing model textbooks on EHV. National Centre for EHV in 
Engineering in IIT, Delhi, and Centre for Leadership and Consciousness in 
Indian Institute of Managment, Lucknow etc. for development of 
courses/programmes for imparting value education have already been set up. 
Some other national level bodies are also in the process of setting up centres 
for value education. Separate Departments of Human Consciousness and 
Yogic Science are being set up in ten selected universities. All the universities 
in the country have been requested to consider setting up a course on Applied 
Philosophy.

Statement 
Details of action taken by Drug Controller (Delhi) to curb the problem of 
spurious/fake drugs 
The Drugs Control Department takes the following measures to contain 
the problem of spurious drugs. 
1. Routine inspection, special inspections and raids in manufacturing 
premises and sale outlets are carried out from time to time. Officers 
of Drugs Control Department, Government of India, are sometime 
associated in raids and special inspections. 
2. Samples of drugs are drawn at random to have a test check on the 
quality of drugs moving in the market. Samples of drugs are test 
purchased through decoy customer and watchers from chemists in 
Delhi and are got screened immediately. In case there is doubt about 
quality of drugs, the premises from where the samples were taken are 
raided and appropriate action is taken. 
3. Complaints received in the Department about quality of drugs arc 
investigated immediately and appropriate action is taken. 
4. Activities of persons of doubtful nature are kept under surveillance. 
5. Liaison is maintained with local people to check and stop 
movements of drugs of doubtful quality through unauthorised and 
illicit channels. 
6. Close liaison is also maintained with the manufacturers and dealers 
of repute with a view to obtaining information against movement, if 
any, of drugs of doubtful quality. 
7. An   Advisory   Committee    has   been   constituted   by   the 
department to increase the public participation for efficient 
enforcement.  The  Committee consists of representatives of 
Indian Medical Association, Delhi Medical Association, All 
India Small  Scale Drugs Manufacturers Association  (Delhi 
Branch).   Chemists   Association   and   Voluntary   Consumer 
Forums.

Control Deptt., Government of India arc sometimes associated in

quality of drugs the premises from where the samples were taken are

channels.

of repute with a view to obtaining information against movement, if 
any, of drugs of doubtful quality.

2848. SHRI    SANJAY    NIRUPAM:     Will    the    Minister    of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that more than 1000 Owls are trapped and killed

magicians? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI 
T.R.BAALU : (a) to (c) Isolated incidents of illegal trapping and killing of

against the offenders on detection of such cases. The steps taken by the 
Government for protection of this species arc as follows: 
62 

[15 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
(i) Hunting of Owl is prohibited under the provisions of Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
(ii) A network of 566 wildlife protected areas covering 4.6% of country's 
geographical area has been created for conservation of wild flora 
and fauna which has helped in protecting the habitat of Owls. 
(iii) Officers arc legally empowered under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 
1972 to detain and arrest the offenders, seize the vehicles, tools, 
animal and animal articles etc. 
(iv) Financial assistance is provided to the State Governments for 
development and management of the protected areas. Raids arc 
conducted by wildlife authorities to curb poaching and illegal trade 
of wild animals. 
(v) International trade in wildlife and its products has been regulated 
under the provisions of CITES (Convention on International Trade in 
Endangered Species). Export of all forms of wild animals including 
their parts and products is prohibited under the EXIM policy. 
(vi) Regional and sub-regional offices of Wildlife Preservation have been 
set up at the main export centres of the country of prevent smuggling 
of wildlife products. 
(vii) Stringent penalties are imposed on the offenders for contravention of 
the provisions of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

year old Tiger and 18 year old Leopard in Sepahijala Zoo, which is located 
within the Sepahijala Sanctuary. No wild Tigers are found in this sanctuary. 
(b) The action taken by the Government to safeguard against death in zoos 
are as follows; 
—Government of India has established Central Zoo Authority under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 with the objective of enforcing standards 
for housing, upkeep and health care of zoo animals. Central Zoo Rules 
have also been incorporated under Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 
providing standards and norms for the upkeep, housing and health care 
of animals in the zoos. 
—A three pronged strategy has been devised for improvement of zoos in 
the country— 
(a) To stop establishment of sub-standard zoos in future. 
(b) To close the zoos where the possibility of bringing the status of 
management of zoo animals to the prescribed standards does not exist. 
(c) To provide technical and financial assistance to the zoos which 
have potential to improve and come upto the prescribed standards. 
Since its enception the Central Zoo Authority has provided financial 
assistance of Rs. 27.48 crores to various zoos for the improvement of 
animal housing, upkeep, health care facility, veterinary care and rescue 
centres. 
- Central Zoo Authority has organised regular courses with Wildlife 
Institute of India, Dehra Dun for capacity building and grading the skills 
of zoo managers, zoo supervisors and zoo veterinarians. They have also 
been sent to small courses to Jersy Wildlife Preservation Trust, U.K. for 
exposure to zoo management in the developed countries. 
- Since the inception of Central Zoo Authority, 23 mobile zoos have 
been closed. 
- All the zoos having lions and tigers in their collection have been 
asked to carry out screening of these animals for blood borne diseases 
and to take preventive and prophylactic action and to avoid 
overcrowding-transfer animals to other zoos. 
- Zoo authorities have been directed to beef up the security.

Illegal trade in animal parts 
2862. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the serious ecological imbalance 
owing to flourishing international market of the dead bodies of almost every 
indian animal species; 
(b) if so, the action taken against the mafia controlling such business; and 
(c) the action proposed against illegal trade in animal parts? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) It is true that poaching and illegal trade of wildlife and its 
derivatives by the organised mafia has serious implications for the 
conservation of wildlife in the country. Poachers have, over the years, 
developed strong linkages with international mafia. They take full advantage 
of the increased conflict between man and wildlife and instigate the villagers 
to poach or assist in poaching those animals that fetch very high price in the 
international clandestine market. They also take advantage of the inadequate 
infra-structural facilities of the forest department outside the protected areas. 
The problem is also compounded by the degradation of the habitat of wild 
animals due to increase in the human and cattle population in and around the 
protected areas. The important wildlife  products traded illegally from the 
country by the organised gangs include Musk, Rhino horns, Bear bile, 
Elephant tusk, Tiger skin and bones and Leopard skin and bones and 
Shahtoosh. 
Government of India has taken following measures against these mafias for 
controlling such illegal activities:— 
(i) Regional and sub-regional offices for wildlife preservation in major 
export and trade centers in the country have been set up to prevent 
smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(ii) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting 
and commercial exploitation under the provisions of Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
(iii) Central Bureau of Investigation has been empowered under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute offenders 
involved in illegal activities. 
(iv) Government of India provides financial and technical help to the  
States  under various  Centrally  Sponsored Scheme   viz.

Project  Tiger,  Project  Elephant,   Development of National Parks   and   
Sanctuaries,   Eco-Development   in   and   Around Protected  Areas,  
Beneficially Oriented Tribal Development Programme etc. for enhancing the

2873. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

in incidence of Malaria in the country; 
(b) if so, the State-wise progress thereof; 
(c) whether the National Malaria Eradication Programme has 
 
 
 
99

RAJYA SABHA      [15 December, 2000] 
not   made   any   significant   progress   in   Orissa,   Chhattisgarh   and 
Jharkhand; 
(d) if so, the steps taken to identify the deficiency; and 
(e) the steps taken to make the NMEP a success? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) As per reports received 
from the State Health Authorities upto 25th November, 2000, the overall 
Malaria situation in the country has shown a decrease by 11.18% in total 
Malaria cases and 4.02% in P.f. cases respectively as compared to the 
corresponding period of 1999. A decline in mortality due to Malaria has also 
been recorded. A Statement showing the incidence of Malaria, P.f. cases and 
deaths due to Malaria during 2000 (as per reports received upto 25.11.2000) 
and that of. corresponding period of 1999, State-wise, is given (See below). 
(c) to (e) As per reports received fr om the State Health Authorities upto 
September, 2000, increase in total Malaria cases and P.f. cases and by 
19.92% and 21.09% respectively has been recorded in Orissa as compared to 
the corresponding period of 1999. 
Epidemiological situation as per reports received upto September, 2000, 
indicates that in Chhattisgarh, there has been an increase by 23.51% in 
Malaria cases and 35.49% in P.f. cases as compared to the corresponding 
period of 1999. 
Increase by 36.92% in Malaria cases and 17.83% in P.f. cases respectively 
upto September, 2000 has been reported in Jharkhand as compared to the 
corresponding period of 1999. 
Following steps are being taken to prevent and control Malaria in the 
country:— 
•   Intensification of early detection and prompt treatment of Malaria 
including treatment of complicated cases by newer drugs. 
 
100 

[15 December, 2000]       RAJYA SABHA 
• Intensification of vector control measures through prioritization of areas 
for selective spray with appropriate insecticides and alternative and 
integrated vector control methods. 
• Introduction of newer insecticides like Synthetic Pyrethroids for selective 
use as per technical requirements. 
• Intensification of Information Education and Communication (IEC) 
activities for public awareness and community participation. 
• Institutional and management capacity building, manpower development 
through intensive re-orientation training programmes at all levels and 
efficient Management Information System (MIS). 
• Implementation of an Enhanced Malaria Control Project (EMCP) with 
World Bank support under the National Anti Malaria Programme 
(NAMP) since September,1997, covering 1045 Primary Health Centres 
(PHCs) in 100 predominantly tribal highly Malaria-endemic districts in 
the peninsular States namely Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Gujarat, 
Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh 
and 19 cities/towns having high endemicity of Malaria in these States 
and the States of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal for 
intensification of Malaria control activities by way of additional inputs 
through a mix of interventions. 
• Providing 100% Central assistance to the 7 North Eastern States since 
December, 1994 under NMEP. 
For intensification of Malaria control activities in the predominantly 
tribal districts reporting high incidence of Malaria and P.f. cases, 21 districts 
in Orissa, 7 districts in Chhattisgarh and 10 districts in Jharkhand are covered 
under the Enhanced Malaria Control Project.

Mechanism for Drug Testing 
2878. SHRI SURESH KALMADI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the country blindly apes the developed 
countries in banning or permitting sale of medicines that arc detrimental for 
health of the people; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether our Drug Control authorities do not have any mechanism 
to either analyse the efficacy of a drug or its harmful effects on the people of 
the country; and 
(d) if so, what steps Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) No, Sir. The. license to 
manufacture and market any approved drug is vested in the Licensing 
auhtorities appointed under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act in the States/Union 
Territories. However, the approval to manufacture or market new drugs is 
given by the Drugs Controller (India), in accordance with the provisions of 
schedule Y of the Drugs & Cosmetics Rules 1945. Banning of any drug is 
also done by the Central Government in consultation with the Drug 
Technical Advisory Board (DTAB), in accordance with the provisions of 
Section 10A, of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, in case of import, and Section 
26 A, in case of manufacture, sale and distribution of any drug. 
(c) and (d) Before approval is given for manufacturing or marketing a 
new drug, data on its safety, efficacy and quality, as well as from animal 
trials and clinical trials on human beings are examined in consultation with 
experts. 
In the case of existing drugs, their screening is a continuous 
107 

RAJYA SABHA       [15 December, 2000] 
process. Based on inputs received from various sources like the WHO, 
experts, professional bodies, etc. such drugs, including drugs banned in-
other-countries are examined by expert committees. The recommendations of 
the expert committee are in turn examined by the DTAB, the statutory body 
that advises Government on technical matters, and based on their 
recommendation, a decision is taken to prohibit manufacture and sale of 
drugs considered ineffective or irrational under Section 26A of the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act. So far 62 categories of drugs and fixed dose combinations of 
drugs have been notified as banned from time to time.

Controlling Spurious Drugs 
2890. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether problems of lack of uniformity and quality assurance 
in    drug   standards,    spurious   drugs    and    inadequacies    in    the 
implementing and monitoring machinery continue to undermine the efficacy 
of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act; 
(b) if so. whether the ministry has proposed some amendments to the 
Drugs and Cosmetic Rules; 
(c) whether an expert committee has been constituted as per the 
Supreme Court directives and the National Human Rights Commission, to 
weedout spurious drugs from the market; and 
(d) to what extent Ministry has obtained help from State 
Governments to tone up the said Act? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Under the provisions of the 
Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Rules thereunder, the responsibility for 
regulating the manufacture and sale of drugs as well as monitoring their 
q u a li ty  is vested with the State Governments. Hence the level of 
infrastructure available to implement the provisions of the said Act and 
Rules made thereunder, also varies from State to State, leading at times to 
lack of uniformity in implementing these provisions. 
(b) No, Sir. Adequate provisions are currently available under the Act 
to ensure the quality of drugs. 
(c) There has been no such directive either from the Supreme Court or 
from the National Human Rights Commission for setting up a committee to 
weed out spurious drugs.

(d) The role of the Central Government is primarily in the realm of 
policy making and in ensuring uniformity in the implementation of the Act 
and the Rules made thereunder, through proper co-ordination. States are 
advised from time to time to strengthen their infrastructure and monitoring 
mechanism, to achieve more effective implementation of the Act. Action 
taken by the states is influenced to a great extent by the capacity and level of 
infrastructure available with them to implement the provisions of the Act and 
the Rules thereunder.

2900. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): India and the US have signed two 
agreements for collaboration research on prevention of HIV/AIDS and 
Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STD) and on maternal and child health and 
Human Development Research. The joint statements were signed on 13th 
June, 2000. 
Under the Indo-US collaboration on prevention of HIV/AIDS and 
Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STD), scientists from the United States and 
India plan to initiate and expand a range of HIV/AIDS and (STD) prevention 
research efforts. These include-behavioural change focussed on a range of

at risk groups; epidemiological research; reproductive health research; 
strategies to prevent perinatal transmission; STD treatment; operational 
research on HIV/AIDS and STD scrviees and AIDS vaccine development. 
The Indo-US collaboration on maternal and child health and Human 
Development Research focuses on areas related to prevention and treatment 
of leading causes of maternal, neonatal and pacdiatric morbidity and 
mortality. The areas of specific interest arc prevention and treatment of low 
birth weight and intrauterine growth retardation; maternal and child nutrition 
and the role of micronutrients  in  healthy child  bearing and adolescent  
health and

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): 
(a) The National Council for Educational Research and Training (NCERT) 
has brought out the National Curriculum Framework for School Education. It 
has been circulated to all the States/Union Territories for implementation of 
the suggestions. 
(b) and (c) After holding regional seminars attended by representatives 
from all sections of society, students, NGOs, administrators, social workers 
etc., the NCERT finalises the National Curriculum Framework. The National 
Framework for School Education was prepared by a Curriculum Group 
established within the NCERT under the chairmanship of the Director 
(NCERT). 
(d) While the framework responds to many new Societal and 
pedagogical changes it remains well within the broad parameters of the 
National Policy on Education framed in 1986 and modified in 1992, some of 
the salient features of the new curriculum framework 
154

are—viewing the child as a constructor of knowledge, reducing the 
curriculum load, using cultural specific pedagogy, universalisation of 
elementary education and linking education with life skills, meeting the 
challenges of information and technology, recognising the interface between 
cognition, emotion and action and evolving a humane, learner, friendly, error 
free, responsive and transparent evaluation system.

about the implementation of the new Curriculum.

Prediction System (COMAPS) program in 1999. The program 
consisted of current and tide measurements and water quality

meteorological parameters (winds, air temperature, humidity and 
atmospheric pressure) and current profiles of water column 0-1000 
m was carried out.

(c) The important steps taken by the Government to check accidents in 
future are listed below:— 
(i) Fouling Mark to Fouling Mark (FM to FM) track circuiting on

commissioned on Mumbai suburban sections of Mumbai. 
(iv) A pilot project of AWS on trial basis for Tughlakabad-Mathura

150 block sections and is being progressively added.

and control.

trains for faster and better means of communication.

based electronic flashing lamps which have better visibility than 
the conventional kerosene lit hand signal lamps. 
(ix) There has been progressive increase in use of Tie Tamping and 
ballast cleaning machines for track maintenance. Also , Track 
Renewal Trains are being used. 
(x) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of the 
track, sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and 
portable accelerometers are being used progressively. 
(xi) For detection of rail fractures-weld failures, adequate double rail 
Ultrasonic Flaw detectors have been procured., Now Self Propelled 
Ultrasonic Rail Testing Cars are being procured. 
(xii) Maintenance facilities for coaches and wagons have been 
modernised and upgraded at many depots. 
(xiii) Routine Over Hauling Depots have been equipped with ultrasonic 
testing equipment for detection of flaws in the axles so as to 
prevent cases of cold breakage of axles. 
(xiv) Whistle Boards / speed breakers and road signs have been provided 
at unmanned lebel crossings and visibility for drivers has been 
improved. 
(xv) Audio-visual publicity campaigns to educate road users on how to 
make a safe crossing are conducted. 
(xvi) Level crossings having heavy traffic density are being progressively 
interlocked with signals on a planned basis. 
(xvii) Training facilities for drivers, guards and staff connected with train 
operation have been modernised including use of simulators for 
training of drivers.

for   Northeast    Frontier    Railway.    Trial    of

(c) 743 passengers were travelling in the train. 
(d) There was no casualty in this accident. 
(e) There was no delay in taking up rescue work. 
(f) Yes, Sir. 
(g) Following steps have been taken to check recurrence of such 
accidents:— 
(i) Intensive inspection of track at supervisors and senior officers level is 
undertaken to ensure round the clock safety. 
(ii) maintenance corridors have been provided on all the trunk route and 
main line sections. Integrated maintenance Blocks are being 
regularly provided for various maintenance work in order to ensure 
that no aspect of safety is neglected due to lack of maintenance. 
(iii) Joint Inspection of Points and Crossings by the Permanent Way and 
Signal Inspectors is being emphasized for improving the 
maintenance standards in this vulnerable area. 
(iv) Intensive footplate inspections to monitor the safe working and 
driving techniques of crew. 
(v) USFD testing of rails and welds at more frequent intervals in the 
critical sections. 
(vi) Regular patrolling of the railway track by Gangmen is carried out 
during vulnerable seasons such as summer, monsoon and the winter 
months. These patrolmen ensure that safety is not endangered by 
buckling, flash floods or rail fractures. 
(vii) Special drives are launched to ensure safe working of staff and 
machines. 
(viii) Stringent penalty to the extent of dismissal/removal from service is 
being imposed on staff held responsible for causing accidents.

Details of the irregulaties in  Group  D  rccrueitments in  the Railways 
1. The contents of the News item are not  based on facts.

manageable number which will be approximately 40 to 70 times the number 
of vacancies available for recruitment in various categories for which 
candidates would be called for viva voce.

2989. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the reaction of Government about India's dismal 
performance at Olympics; 
(b) whether this reflects poor economic condition of our country, 
compared with China, Japan, Korea and many other countries; and 
(c) if   so,   whether,   in   spite   of   poor   economic   condition.

Government are considering for a special fund to develop sports through 
MPLAD? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI P. 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) and (b) The performance of the Indian Contingent 
in the Sydney Olympics was unsatisfactory in terms of medals secured, 
particularly when compared with the performance of China, Japan and Korea. 
However, relative to the earlier performance at the Atlanta Olympics, the 
performance by India in many disciplines such as Boxing, Women's 
Weightlifting, Judo and Shooting was better. 
Better economic conditions and higher per capita investment in sports 
are certainly factors contributing to higher performance in sports by countries 
like Japan and Korea, while in China State control of sports and a large 
infrastructural base have contributed to the performance of Chinese sports-
persons in various international competit ions. In contrast, India suffers from 
a poor sports infrastructure base due to inadequate budgetary allocations for 
sports, both at the Centre and in the States. 
(c) There is no proposal with the Government for a special fund to 
develop sports through MPLAD. However, Hon'ble Members of Parliament 
are free to use funds from the MPLAD scheme for the development of sports 
infrastructure in their respective constituencies.

Threat caused by the 10 Cracks Developed In Koyna Dam 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, Koyna 
Dam situated on the Krishna river in Satara District of Maharashtra has 
recently developed cracks due to the earthquake, resulting in water 
leakage at the rate of 2,400 litres per minute. Besides that, in 
October, a large quantity of water was discharged, causing a lot of 
anxiety in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. The water storage 
capacity of Koyna Dam is around 85 TMC ft. This is one of the larger 
dams, and the water stored in the dam is used primarily for power 
generation and irrigation purposes. The people of both Karnataka and 
Andhra Pradesh are very much worried about the cracks and the 
possible threat, from the dam, to their lives and property. Major 
irrigation projects such as the Almatti in Karnataka and Nagarjuna 
Sagar and Srisailam in Andhra Pradesh will be in great danger, if the 
dam bursts. Nagarjuna and Srisailam are two mighty reservoirs with a 
storage capacity of around 350 TMC ft. each and are providing 
irrigation facilities to lakhs of hect ares of land and generating a large 
quantity of electricity in the State of Andhra Pradesh. Once the dam 
bursts, all the towns and villages situated on the banks of river 
Krishna in the lower riparian States of Karnataka and Andhra 
Pradesh, will be washed away, resulting in a huge loss to human life 
and property. This is going to be a very major catastrophe. Sir, a 
week ago, this area was, again, rocked by an earthquake with a 
magnitude of 3.5 on the Richter scale. It appears that the 
Maharashtra Government is not taking the issue seriously. The Chief 
Engineer of the Dam took it lightly, and he is very callous in this 
regard. But Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka are worried because the 
river flows through the breadth of the States. 
It is requested that the Central Government and the Central 
Water Commission should take the matter very seriously, convene a 
meeting of the three States and resolve the issue immediately,

Open Indo-Nepal Border Adversely Affecting National Security 
SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN (Uttar Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, 
Sir, I am grateful to you for permitting me to mention a matter of 
urgent public importance relating to the open Indo-Nepal border which 
is adversely affecting the national security. 
Sir, the open nature of the Indo-Nepal border facilitates the 
launching of anti-India operations by the ISI of Pakistan from the soil 
of Nepal. The militant groups, with the assistance of the Pak ISI 
agents, are continuously infiltrating into India through the porous Indo-
Nepal border and we are unable to curb it. They are taking shelter in 
various towns of Uttar Pradesh, North-Eastern States, Punjab and, 
particularly, Delhi. Whatever has been done to counter such activities 
has not produced the desired results and it is yet to be curbed. Our 
intelligence machinery on the border s is very poor. The number of 
outposts for checking infiltration is very few. There is a need to 
increase the number of outposts of security forces. Unless we 
increase the number of these outposts, it will be very difficult to check 
these things. Apart from that, the police and the paramilitary forces 
manning these outposts do not have modern weapons. This is very 
important.   Unless they have modern weapons, how can they

counter such activities? They are not having sophisticated weapons. 
These militants are using Indo-Nepalese passports and many of them 
are not even using passports. Since passports are not needed, the 
undesirable and criminal elements are entering into India without 
proper checking. Some kind of checking is being done at some 
places. But the number of such places on the border is very few. 
There is a need to re-examine how such activities can be curbed. 
Although talks have been held at the Home Secretaries level in 
Kathmandu in the month of July, Nepal has not done much that was 
expected of them. Today, Nepal has become an important base-camp 
for Pak-supported ISI activities. Although Nepal has promised that 
they would counter such activities, which are inimical to India's 
interests, they have not done much on this issue. The ISI agents are 
infiltrating into India freely with arms and indulging in subversive 
activities in the North-East, Kashmir, Uttar Pradesh and other places. 
A detailed statement from the Government is needed so that the 
nation may know as to what the Government has in mind to curb 
these anti-India opeiations from the soil of Nepal.

SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI (Tamil Nadu): Sir, the strike 
launched by the E.D.A. and postal employees has crossed ten days. 
This indefinite strike has affected the postal service across the 
country. Sir, we were told that the last strike that took place in July, 
1998, was withdrawn on a specific agreement reached between the 
Government and the Joint Council of Action comprising all important 
labour unions. We were further informed that the Government had 
agreed to implement the recommendations of Justice Talwar 
Committee for E.D.A., enhancement of salary to Group 'D' employees, 
and revision of salary at Rs.3,050 on Time Bound One Promotion 
(TBOP) and Rs.3,200 on B.C.R. for Group 'D'. The Joint Council of 
Action demanded Rs.3,050 plus for postmen with retrospective effect 
from 1.1.96. The salaries demanded for postmen were Rs.4,000 on 
TBOP and Rs.5,000 on BCR. For Class III employees, the JCOA 
demanded Rs.5,500 on TBOP and Rs.6,500 on BCR. They also 
demanded promotion of ten per cent employees as HSGI from BCR 
list. We have been informed that these demands were already agreed 
to by the Government of India. If  this is so, then, the Government 
should issue necessary orders to implement their demands. 
Otherwise, the Government should inform this House, the full details 
about the agreement reached with labour unions. The postal 
employees have been agitating over these issues since 1993. We feel 
that these demands are genuine. The Delhi High Court has also 
directed the Government to end this impasse on or before 20th 
December. We urge upon the Government to find an amicable

SHRI CO. POULOSE (Kerala): Mr. Chairman, Sir, the NTC 
was set up with the main objective of managing the affairs of the sick 
textile undertakings taken over by the Government to safeguard the 
employment of workers. At the time  of nationalisation, a large number

was spent on modernisation which was grossly inadequate. So the

turnaround plan for the revival of 79 mills and merger of 36 mills in the 
18 mills was adopted in 1995.  Even after

PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Sir, The 
Hindu newspaper carried out a news item on 4th December, 2000, 
indicating that the Department of Posts, in order to celebrate the 5000-
year old tradition of Indian jewellery, has issued six commemorative 
stamps on gems and jewellery, covering three distinct categories - 
basic daily ornaments, ceremonial jewellery and spectacular jewels of 
gods and kings. I have several questions to put before the hon.  
Minister for Communications. 
288 

[15 December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA  
Firstly, why is the Department of Posts commemorating Indian 
jewellery? True, India's export trade in gems and jewellery slowed 
down in 2000-01, and its contribution to total exports came down to 16 
per cent from 18 per cent. But, issuing stamps on jewellery designs 
cannot be clear on small pieces of paper and hardly increases the 
exports. It will generate interest and demands at home. Further, it 
increases consumerism and, most importantly, block the money spent 
on gems and gold. The same could have been used for productive 
forms of investment. The Minister mentioned on 28 th November, in 
reply to an Unstarred Question, I quote, "Important national and 
international events are considered for issue of stamps." Which 
important event which justifies this issue? He also mentioned, 
"popular themes" for stamps. Yes, jewellery is popular, sadly, with the 
Indian women. But, there are themes of art and culture, like 
handicrafts, Indian classical music and dance. Why should we spend 
money on advertising jewellery through stamps? Sir, Begum Rokeye 
Sakhewat Hussain, said in 1905, I quote, "Do not invest on jewellery 
for your daughters. Spend money on their education." The 
Government sponsored schemes, which popularise expensive 
jewellery, are against the women's real interest. I urge upon the hon. 
Minister not to pursue the project. Export gems and jewellery - 
unproductive products - abroad and earn foreign exchange, but do not 
encourage domestic consumerism on unproductive things which are 
against women's real interest. 
Need to control bureaucratic corruption and red tape and 
streamlining the decision making process 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): Recently, the 
Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) organized a meeting with the 
diplomatic fraternity to attract foreign direct investments into the 
country. In that meeting, 40 Ambassadors of various . countries were' 
present. Surprisingly, the diplomats were unanimously against a 
single bugbear, namely, the Indian bureaucracy, which has its strange 
ways and it is the main hurdle due to which overseas companies and 
entrepreneurs do not invest in India through their enterprises. They 
felt that there is rampant corruption in the bureaucracy followed by 
inadequate infrastructure, which is hampering the FDI in India. Some 
of them felt that foreign investors are interested only in those States, 
which are headed by the I.T.-savvy Chief Ministers. One diplomat 
complained that the Income-tax Authorities in our country are 
harassing the companies of his country, which is working as a 
deterrent for others in his country. They felt that if corruption and other 
bureaucratic hurdles are removed, India could attract substantial FDI. 
 
289 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2000]  
Hence, there is need to control the bureaucratic corruption 
and red tape and streamlining the decision-making process. At the 
same time, officers responsible for decision-making be given more 
autonomy to ensure accountability. The system of reporting by officers 
to Ministers, PMO, CVC, Parliament and various Committees also 
need to be minimized so that they take decisions   freely   and 
fearlessly, but with accountability.

SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN (Kerala): I rise to support the 
Resolution moved by the hon. Shri Nagendra Nath Ojha requesting 
the Government to pass a comprehensive legislation for the 
agricultural workers. While moving this Resolution, the Mover of the 
Resolution explained the history behind this piece of legislation. A Bill 
is pending before Parliament for the last twenty-five years. Actually, 
the hon. Labour Minister will get an opportunity to celebrate the Silver 
Jubilee of this Bill which is pending before Parliament. Why could not 
this piece of legislation be enacted by Parliament during the la^t 
twenty-five years? What was the reason? 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI) in the Chair] 
This issue has to be addressed properly. I would like to know. 
Who are opposing this Bill? That is the question. The Mover has 
explained, in detail, about the various Committees and attempts that 
were made with regard to this Bill. 
In the last meeting of the State Labour Ministers, the Central 
Government circulated a background paper. In that background paper 
it was revealed that 35 consultations and meetings were held with 
regard to this Bill. It is just moving from the State Labour Ministers 
Conference to the Cabinet and then back to the State Labour 
Ministers, then back to the State, then again, back to the State Labour 
Ministers' Conference, then

Commission. I do not know the reason behind this. I do not know what 
kind of hurdles, the Government has to cross, with regard to this Bill. 
What does it reveal? It reveals the bias towards the rich people and 
landlords, in the society. That is the reason. This Parliament 
represents the landlords rather than the poor people of this country. 
That is the reason. Why is it happening? It has been discussed, time 
and again. Now, the problems are increasing, not decreasing for the 
agricultural workers. If you look at the graph of the number of

other parts of the world, the percentage of agricultural workers is from 
5 per cent to 10 per cent, but, in our country, it has been increasing

helping to enhance the number of agricultural workers in the country, 
but, not helping to reduce it. After liberalisation, what is happening? 
Now, what is the situation in rural India? Sir, every year, nearly, two 
crores of agricultural workers are migrating. They are migrating from 
one State to the other. This year, it has been reported that agricultural 
workers are migrating from Orissa. I think, the Railway Minister will be

Information Technology. How can we survive without food? Someone

workers are forced to migrate from villages to towns. This itself is 
creating problems. 
With regard to agricultural workers, I would like to submit that 
half of the agricultural workers consist of females. The agricultural 
workers who are migrating are mostly males. Now, what is the 
situation? These poor female workers are forced to look after their 
entire family. Then, you talk about the literacy and other things. 
Will it be possible for the children of the agricultural labourers 
to go to schools? No, that will not possible. Again, this Government 
has decided to enhance the prices of food articles distributed through 
the PDS. What is this going on? Because of that attitude, because of 
that myopic attitude of this Government, the off-take is reducing like 
anything. Sir, if you go through the figures of the off-take from the PDS 
shops in the first

speech, but it was not continuous. However, I enjoyed his speech to a 
great extent. I would request the hon. Member to go through the 
Ministry of Labour's Annual Report, 1999. In that report, it has been 
mentioned I quote "Since there have been divergent views on various 
components of the proposed legislatio n for the welfare of agricultural 
workers from different States/UTs, a Conference of the Labour 
Ministers' of States/UTs was organised under the Chairpersonship of 
the Union Labour Minister on 18.1.2000, with a view to reaching a 
consensus in the matter." I submit that, even today, we have not 
reached a consensus. I request the hon. Labour Minister to let this 
august House know as to whether any consensus has been arrived at 
with regard to a legislation for the agricultural labourers. For the last 
50 years, we have not been able to do it. I hope, at least, in the next 
session, we would be able to achieve it and a legislation will be 
brought forth in the august House. 
Agricultural workers consist of the largest segment of the 
workers in the unorganised sector. The number, according to the 
1991 Census, was 74.6 million. In addition, a significant number-
110.7 million listed as cultivator s and another 6 million listed as 
engaged in allied activities, particularly those having very small 
holdings (large, medium and small farmers) may also come under the 
definition of agricultural labourers. There is no law for them even now. 
The social condition, the economic condition, of these people is poor. 
They are living in poverty. They are living as illiterates. They live like 
bonded labour as my learned friend has pointed out.   In order to 
eradicate poverty, in order to remove illiteracy and in order

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2000] 
to come out of the clutches of the bonded labour, this sort of 
legislation is essential. The problem of agricultural labourers and their 
unemployment and poverty has to be tackled meticulously by this 
Government. They should be provided with infrastructural facilities, 
financial assistance, diversification to non-farm activities, etc. The 
Government should take steps to generate employment and bring 
poverty alleviation schemes for them. Different States have enacted 
different laws. But that is not sufficient. There should be a centralised 
legislation by this Government in order to help the agriculturists. A 
welfare fund should be created. The fund should provide for social 
amenities like health and medical care. Broadly, the problem of 
agricultural labourers can be classified into two groups. They are; 
social problems and economic problems. Since agricultural labourers 
are living in rural areas, this is a social problem for them. Economic 
problems arise due to inadequate employment opportunities, low 
income and inadequate diversification of economic activities in rural 
areas. So, in order to eradicate the economic problems and social 
problems, we are in need of a legislation at present. 
I submit further that as far as women labourers are 
concerned, their condition is very, very poor. They are paid only 60 
per cent of the wages earned by men. Poverty and illiteracy force 
them to borrow money, from time to time, from private money-lenders. 
They have been consigned to borrow for social obligations like 
celebration of marriages of their sons and daughters. In order to get 
money, they have to become bonded labourers.   They are working as 
bonded labourers with rich people. 
Here, I would like to bring to the notice of this august House a 
scheme brought by the Tamil Nadu Government. The State of Tamil 
Nadu has been a pioneer in that. A welfare fund has been created by 
the Government of Tamil Nadu. I think 64 categories of employees 
have been included in it. The scheme is being inaugurated tomorrow. 
According to the scheme that Dr. Kalaignar, the Chief Minister of 
Tamil Nadu, has announced, Rs.One lakh is given to the labourers for 
the marriages of their sons and daughters and Rs.One lakh is given 
for the education of children. In the wh ole of India, this is the first time 
that such a scheme has been launched. Even West Bengal has not 
done it. Therefore, I thought I would take this opportunity to mention it. 
Finally, this sort of legislation which is in the interests of 
agricultural labourers is very necessary. I am highly thankful to Mr. 
Ojha for bringing this legislation. I welcome it. Thank you very much.
